第1-2题: The Brant Institute has confirmed that a soft-bodied animal filmed in the Vellin Trench is a species previously unknown to science. The trench lies roughly four thousand metres below the surface of the southern Ardic Ocean, where sunlight never reaches and the water stays close to freezing. The creature, about the length of a human thumb, was first recorded three years ago by a camera mounted on a remotely operated vehicle. At the time, the team assumed it was a familiar species that had drifted far outside its normal range. Genetic comparison with two specimens collected last summer, however, showed differences too large to set aside, and the animal has now been formally described. Researchers say it feeds on bacteria that cluster around mineral vents, and that its shell has almost entirely disappeared, an adaptation that saves energy in water where calcium is scarce. A full account will appear in the institute's journal next month.
第3-4题: The city of Halden will remove private cars from its historic centre from the first week of April, after a council vote that ended almost two years of argument. The zone covers some forty streets around the old harbour, an area that currently handles about eighteen thousand vehicle movements a day. Delivery vans will still be admitted before ten in the morning, and residents holding a parking permit will keep access to their own street. The council has funded two new tram stops and a fleet of small electric buses that will circle the zone every eight minutes. Traders had warned that the change would push shoppers towards retail parks on the edge of the city, and the final vote was close. Officials say noise and air quality will be monitored for a full year, and that the findings will be published before the scheme is reviewed.
第5-7题: Ellsworth University has given every first-year student access to an artificial intelligence assistant that answers questions about course material at any hour of the day. The system was trained on lecture notes, reading lists and past examination papers, and it is designed to reply in ordinary language rather than send students to a page number. Officials describe it as a supplement to tutorials, not a replacement for them. In a trial last term involving four thousand students, those who used the assistant at least once a week were slightly more likely to submit assignments on time, although the university warns that the difference may say more about study habits than about the tool itself. Teaching staff may switch the assistant off for their own modules, and about one in five has done so. A student survey found wide approval, but also complaints that the system sometimes gave confident answers that were simply wrong.
第8-11题: Ms. Aldridge: Come in, Lena. Sit down. How are you feeling now that the ten weeks are over?
Lena: Honestly? A bit strange. Everyone else on the team is staying, and I'm clearing my desk.

Ms. Aldridge: Well, not quite clearing it. That's partly why I asked you in. First, the feedback. Your research was the strongest of any intern we've had this year. The market summary you did in week three is still being passed around.
Lena: That's good to hear. I was worried it was too long.
Ms. Aldridge: It was long. It was also the only one that told us something we didn't already know. Where you struggled, and you know this, was the client meeting in week seven.
Lena: I do. I had twelve slides and about four minutes.
Ms. Aldridge: You had twelve slides and four minutes, and you started with the methodology. Nobody in that room cared about methodology. They cared about whether they could afford the thing.
Lena: I've thought about that a lot since. I keep rehearsing a shorter version.
Ms. Aldridge: Good. Now, the reason I asked you in. There is no full-time position. Not yet. The budget for the design team is frozen until the third quarter, and I can't give you a date.

Ms. Aldridge: That's not it. I can offer you a part-time contract, twenty hours a week, starting in February, on the same account. It isn't what you applied for, and the pay is pro rata, which I know is a step down from what you'd hoped.
Lena: It's a step up from nothing.
Ms. Aldridge: That's the spirit. But I'd like something from you in return. I want you to present at the April review. Ten minutes, no slides, just you and the client.
Lena: Ten minutes with no slides? Can I use one chart?
Ms. Aldridge: One chart. That's the deal.
第12-15题: Dr. Rowe: So, Marcus, you wanted to talk about the proposal.
Marcus: Yes. I've been reading for about six weeks, and I think my topic is too broad. I started with how museums use digital media, which is, I realise now, about four theses.
Dr. Rowe: It is at least four. Which of the four interests you most?

Marcus: The labels. Not the websites, not the social media accounts, but the short descriptions next to the objects. I want to compare how three regional museums write them, and whether the writing changed after the collections went online.
Dr. Rowe: That's manageable. How many objects?
Marcus: That's my problem. One museum has forty thousand records.
Dr. Rowe: Then don't take all of them. Take a sample, say two hundred objects per museum, drawn the same way in each. What would you compare?
Marcus: Length, use of technical terms, whether an object's history is told as a story or as a list of facts. And I'd interview the curators who wrote them.
Dr. Rowe: The interviews will take longer than you think. Curators are, how shall I put this, generous with their time in principle and impossible to schedule in practice.
Dr. Rowe: Budget five. And Marcus, one more thing. You've written whether the writing changed. Changed compared with what?
Marcus: With the labels written before the collections went online. I have access to the old card indexes at two of the three.

Dr. Rowe: Then say so in the proposal, in the first paragraph, not on page nine. The committee reads the first page properly and skims the rest. Also, your literature review is currently nineteen pages.
Marcus: I know. I got carried away.
Dr. Rowe: Cut it to eight. Nobody is impressed by length. They're impressed by a question they can answer.
第16-18题: Ask anyone who works in media what has changed most in the past fifteen years, and the answer is rarely about technology. It is about measurement. A newspaper once knew how many copies it sold; a television channel knew roughly how many people were watching. Neither knew, with any precision, which sentence on which page had lost the reader's interest. Today that information arrives continuously, and it arrives while the work is still being made. Editors can see, minute by minute, where an audience stops scrolling, and they see it early enough to change the next piece.

The effect is not simply that content gets shorter. Length, in fact, has proved surprisingly resilient; long podcasts and lengthy essays still find large audiences. What has changed is the shape of attention. A piece now has to earn the right to be finished, and it has to do so within the first few seconds, because the platform offers an alternative at every moment. The result is a form that front-loads its most striking material, the surprising figure, the blunt claim, the anecdote, and only afterwards supplies the reasoning that would make the claim defensible.

Critics describe this as a corruption of public understanding, and there is something in that. But the criticism is often aimed at the wrong target. Audiences have always preferred to be entertained before they are informed; what is new is that the preference is now visible, countable and immediately profitable. A journalist who resists it is not resisting a machine but a measurable demand, and that is a far harder thing to argue with. The honest question is not whether the attention economy has changed the shape of what we read. It plainly has. The question is who, if anyone, is willing to pay for the version that takes longer.
第19-21题: Urban farming has a persuasive logic. Food grown on a rooftop travels a few hundred metres instead of a few thousand, the roof itself stays cooler, and the grower learns something about where dinner comes from. City governments have noticed, and plots have multiplied, on school grounds, in hospital courtyards and on the flat roofs of supermarkets.

The difficulty is arithmetic. A well-run rooftop farm might produce four or five kilograms of vegetables per square metre in a year. A city of a million people eats, very roughly, seventy thousand tonnes of vegetables annually. To grow even a tenth of that on roofs, you would need several square kilometres of suitably strong, flat, sunlit surface, and cities do not have several square kilometres of it in the places where people actually live. Studies of a number of European and North American cities have reached the same conclusion: the ceiling on roof-based production lies somewhere between one and three per cent of demand, and it is reached long before the land runs out.

None of this makes urban agriculture pointless. Its value is better measured in what it does to people than in what it puts in the shops. A child who has pulled a carrot out of soil understands a supply chain in a way no diagram achieves, and community plots have repeatedly been shown to widen the social contacts of people who would otherwise be isolated. There is also the question of what else the land could be used for; a rooftop garden is a poor substitute for housing, but it is an excellent use of a surface that would otherwise do nothing at all. The mistake is to treat it as a solution to food supply. It is a solution to something else, and that something else deserves to be named clearly.
第22-25题: Why does a song from adolescence stay in the memory when the name of a colleague met last week does not? Part of the answer is repetition: songs are designed to be heard many times, and repetition is the oldest known method of fixing material in the mind. But repetition alone does not explain the peculiar quality of musical memory, which is so often involuntary. A few bars of a tune can return a room, a smell, a person, entire, after decades in which none of it was consciously recalled.

Researchers who study this point to the way music is stored. Words are remembered largely for their meaning; music is remembered in several channels at once, pitch, rhythm, timbre and the physical memory of how it feels to sing or play it. When these channels are laid down together, each becomes a route back to the others, so a single cue can open the whole. This is why a melody heard in childhood can survive damage that has erased the events around it; patients in the later stages of memory loss will sometimes sing every word of a song learned long ago while being unable to say what day it is.

The practical use of this is younger than the science. Care homes have begun running singing groups not as entertainment but as therapy, and staff report that residents who speak very little will join a familiar chorus. The effects do not last long once the music stops, and nobody claims that singing restores memory in any general sense. What it restores is something narrower and, for the person concerned, more immediate: for the length of a verse, the past is not something being described. It is something being done.
